pass_a_gloss: This also is useful toward the things set before us. Solomon in Ecclesiastes says he praised all those who have died above the living, all who are still living until now. Who could be praised so reasonably when dead as the man who by his own choice took on death on behalf of piety? Of that sort was Eleazar, taking on death with good fame rather than life with pollution, and leading himself by his own choice to the torture wheel; or the one who, having taken up a refined reasoning, worthy of his ninety-year age, and of the pre-eminence of old age, and of the acquired and conspicuous grey head, and of the finest rearing from a child, and more than that of the holy lawgiving created by God, said that it is not worthy of our age to play a part, in order that many of the young, having supposed Eleazar the ninety-year-old to have changed over into the foreigners' way, they too because of my play-acting and because of the small and momentary living should be misled because of me, and I shall acquire pollution and stain on old age. For even if for the present I shall take myself out of the punishment from humans, yet the hands of the all-ruler I shall flee neither living nor having died. Therefore, by changing life now in manly fashion I shall appear worthy of old age, and to the young I shall have left behind a noble pattern toward dying well eagerly and nobly on behalf of the solemn and holy laws. I pray you, having come beside the doors of death, or rather of freedom, most of all if pains should be brought on, (for nothing is there to give up expecting that you suffer from the counsel of the opposing powers), to say such things: to the Lord who has the holy knowledge it is manifest that, being able to be loosed from death, I bear hard pains in body being whipped, but in soul I suffer these with pleasure because of fear of him. Such then was Eleazar's death, so that it was said over him: not only to the young but to the most of the nation he has left his own death as a pattern of nobility and a remembrance of virtue.
pass_b_english: This too is useful for our subject. Solomon says in Ecclesiastes, “I praised all the dead above the living, as many as are alive until now” (Ecclesiastes 4:2). Who among the dead could be praised with such good reason as the one who, of his own free choice, accepted death for the sake of godliness? Such a man was Eleazar, who welcomed “death with glory rather than life with defilement” and of his own free will went forward to the rack (2 Maccabees 6:19); or the man who, “taking up a noble resolve worthy of his ninety years, of the eminence of his old age, of his hard-won and distinguished grey hair, of his excellent upbringing from childhood, and still more of the holy legislation established by God” (2 Maccabees 6:23), said:

“It is not worthy of our age to pretend, so that many of the young, supposing that Eleazar at ninety had gone over to foreign ways, should themselves be led astray through me, because of my pretence and for the sake of a brief and fleeting life, while I bring defilement and disgrace on my old age. For even if for the present I escape the punishment that comes from men, I shall not escape the hands of the Almighty, whether alive or dead. So by giving up my life bravely now I shall show myself worthy of my old age, and I shall leave to the young a noble example of how to die a good death, readily and nobly, for the revered and holy laws” (2 Maccabees 6:24-28).

I pray that you, when you come to the doors of death, or rather of freedom, and especially if tortures are brought to bear on you (for there is nothing you can rule out suffering at the will of the hostile powers), may say words like these: “To the Lord, who has holy knowledge, it is plain that, though I could be released from death, I endure harsh pains in my body under the scourge, but in my soul I suffer these things gladly because of my fear of him” (2 Maccabees 6:30). Such, indeed, was Eleazar's death that it was said of him at the last: “Not only to the young but to the greater part of the nation he left his own death as an example of nobility and a memorial of virtue” (2 Maccabees 6:31).

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 22); the old English was a digest: it cut Eleazar's whole speech (2 Macc 6:24-28) and the citation of 6:23 and 6:30, dropped Origen's prayer that his readers may speak like Eleazar at 'the doors of death, or rather of freedom', and added a line ('So we too ... leave children and brethren an example worth more than life') that the Greek does not have.
Koetschau prints ἀνατροφῆς; translated 'upbringing' as printed (2 Maccabees reads 'conduct').
Either gives 'gone over to'; translated 'had gone over to foreign ways'.
